challenges.name: Pit Streak
challenges.note: Nine correct actions in a row

hazards.cartop-edge: You leaned past the car-top rail with the car-top stop switch not yet engaged. The pit switch does not protect someone standing on the car itself — an unswitched car can still answer a call and carry you into the overhead clearance.
hazards.counterweight-zone: You stepped into the counterweight runby without the pit stop-switch confirmed engaged. If the switch is not truly holding the drive, an arriving car or counterweight gives no warning and no time to get clear — crush and shear injuries here are almost always fatal.
hazards.frayed-governor-rope: That governor rope has visibly broken wires that were ignored during inspection. A frayed rope can slip or part before it ever pulls the safeties, which is exactly the failure the governor exists to catch.
hazards.quick-restore-switch: That is a shortcut restore switch, not the proper sequence. Closing it re-energises the car before anyone has confirmed the pit and car top are clear of people and the locks have come off in order.

interrupts.alert: A hall call has registered upstairs. Somebody is standing at a landing pressing the button, and you are in the pit.
interrupts.cue: Prove the switch is still holding the car.
interrupts.missNote: You stayed in the runby with a live call registered and an unconfirmed switch. If that switch had been knocked off its detent on the way in — and they do get knocked — the first warning would have been the counterweight passing your head.
interrupts.why: A registered call is the building telling you it still thinks this car is in service. The pit switch is the only thing between that call and the car coming down on top of you, so it gets confirmed, not assumed.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the pit stop switch. While you are standing in the runby with a call registered, nothing else in this shaft is worth looking at.

interrupts.alert: Somebody at the machine room end has started working your lock off the hasp to run the car for another job.
interrupts.cue: That is your lock and your life on the end of it.
interrupts.missNote: The lock came off while you were on the car top. Everything after that depended on the other mechanic deciding not to press the button — which is not a control, it is a hope.
interrupts.why: One lock, one person, one key, removed by the person who fitted it and nobody else. A lock coming off while you are standing on the car is the exact sequence that the whole procedure exists to make impossible.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the hasp with your lock on it. Stop what you are doing and go to the lock.

lateNotes.cartop-stop-switch: The car-top switch is only reachable once you are already standing on the car — it is not operated from the pit floor below.
lateNotes.governor-instrument: Governor rope condition is only checked once both stop switches are confirmed and the car top is safe to stand on.

name: Elevator Pit

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the permit and confirm the car-out-of-service signage is posted at every landing.
steps.prompt: Read the permit and confirm the car-out-of-service signage is posted at every landing.
steps.title: Open the work permit and post out-of-service
steps.why: Signage goes up at every landing before the disconnect comes down, because the thing that kills elevator mechanics is not the machinery, it is a passenger on the fourth floor who had no way of knowing anybody was in the shaft. A barricaded landing is also the only warning to the next person that the doors may open onto a hoistway with no car behind them.

steps.cue: Grab the machine room's main line disconnect handle and pull it open.
steps.prompt: Grab the machine room's main line disconnect handle and pull it open.
steps.title: Open the main line disconnect
steps.why: The main line disconnect is the isolation for this car and nothing in the pit or on the car top is approached until it is open. It is pulled firmly to its stop rather than eased over, because a switch left between positions can leave one phase made — which is how a drive that is supposed to be dead turns a motor far enough to move a car.

steps.cue: Apply your padlock and tag to the disconnect.
steps.prompt: Apply your padlock and tag to the disconnect.
steps.title: Lock and tag the disconnect
steps.why: One lock, one key, one person, and the key stays in your pocket for the whole job. The lock is what turns an open switch into a legal isolation under the control of hazardous energy standard, and the tag is what tells the building engineer whose car this is and when it will be back. Without the lock the switch is only a switch, and switches get closed by people who are sure nobody is in there.

steps.cue: Meter the drive input and commit when it reads dead.

gauge.label: DRIVE INPUT — VOLTAGE
gauge.missNote: Still reading live. Recheck the disconnect before anyone goes near the pit or the car top.

steps.prompt: Meter the drive input and commit when it reads dead.
steps.title: Verify zero energy at the controller
steps.why: An open disconnect is a claim; the meter is the proof, and it is taken at the drive input where the work is, not at the switch. Prove the instrument live on a known source, take your reading, prove it live again — the live-dead-live sequence is there because a meter with a blown fuse reads zero volts on every busbar in the building, and it reads zero very convincingly.

steps.cue: Confirm the pit stop switch is ON before you set foot on the ladder.
steps.prompt: Confirm the pit stop switch is ON before you set foot on the ladder.
steps.title: Engage the pit stop switch
steps.why: The pit switch is a second, independent way of stopping this car, and the reason the code insists on it is that isolation in a machine room two floors away cannot be seen from the bottom of a hoistway. Reaching in from the landing and throwing it before you commit your weight to the ladder means the thing holding the car is something you can watch while you are underneath it.

steps.cue: Climb down the fixed pit ladder now that the switch is confirmed.
steps.prompt: Climb down the fixed pit ladder now that the switch is confirmed.
steps.title: Descend into the pit
steps.why: Down the ladder, facing it, with the light on — not stepped down onto the buffer or dropped the last part of the way. A pit is a hole with a counterweight runby down one side of it, standing water at the bottom of many of them, and no room to move once you are in, so the way in is the way the code provides and not the short way.

steps.cue: Walk the pit. Three things are wrong — find them by looking.

decoyNotes.secure-rung: That rung is solid and correctly fastened.
decoyNotes.sound-buffer: That buffer is sound — no action needed.

itemNotes.loose-rung: A corroded rung fails exactly when someone puts their full weight on it climbing out in a hurry.
itemNotes.sump-overflow: Standing water in the pit is both a slip hazard and a shock hazard around any pit lighting or wiring.
itemNotes.worn-buffer: A cracked spring buffer cannot absorb an over-travel the way it is rated to — tag it out and replace it before the car runs again.

steps.prompt: Walk the pit. Three things are wrong — find them by looking.
steps.title: Inspect the buffers and pit ladder
steps.why: A pit inspection is a search for what has quietly failed since the last visit, not a checklist ticked from the doorway. Everything down here only matters on the day something else has already gone wrong: the buffer is for an over-travel that should never happen, and the ladder is for the climb out you will be making in a hurry when it does.

steps.cue: Climb to the car top and confirm the car-top stop switch is ON.
steps.prompt: Climb to the car top and confirm the car-top stop switch is ON.
steps.title: Engage the car-top stop switch
steps.why: This is the second independent switch and it protects a different person from the first one. The pit switch protects whoever is in the pit; it does nothing at all for somebody standing on the car, which can still be called away under them by the machine above. The switch goes on before you get on the car, reached from the landing, not once you are already up there.

steps.cue: Open the hatch and set the car to car-top inspection mode.
steps.prompt: Open the hatch and set the car to car-top inspection mode.
steps.title: Open the car-top access and enter inspection mode
steps.why: Inspection mode caps the car's speed, cuts out the door operator and the automatic calls, and moves control to the station under your own hand. It is what turns a passenger lift into a work platform. Without it, everything about this car is still being decided by whoever presses a button in the lobby.

steps.cue: Hold the enable and the run button together and take the car to the next working position.
steps.holdBreakNote: You let go and the car stopped, which is exactly what constant pressure is for. Take it again and hold both controls for the whole move.
steps.prompt: Hold the enable and the run button together and take the car to the next working position.
steps.title: Run the car on constant pressure
steps.why: Inspection operation is constant pressure by design: let go of either button and the car stops within its own length. That is not an inconvenience, it is the safety device — the one thing standing between a mechanic who trips, faints or is struck by something and a car that carries on to the overhead with them on top of it. Riding the car top with anything jammed, taped or wedged on that button is how people are crushed at the top of the shaft.

steps.cue: Read the governor rope tension and commit inside the rated band.

gauge.label: GOVERNOR ROPE — TENSION
gauge.missNote: Outside the rated tension. Adjust and recheck before the car goes back in service.

steps.prompt: Read the governor rope tension and commit inside the rated band.
steps.title: Check the governor rope tension
steps.why: The governor is the device that notices an overspeed and pulls the safeties into the rails, and it can only pull them if the rope is tensioned to grip in the sheave. Slack and it slips, so the safeties never set; over-tensioned and the tension sheave bottoms out in the pit and the rope starts wearing. Both faults look like a rope hanging there perfectly normally, which is why this is read off an instrument.

steps.cue: Release the car-top switch, then the pit switch, then take your lock off the hasp, then close the main disconnect.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Wrong order — car-top switch, then pit switch, then your lock, and the main disconnect last. The lock is the last thing off and the disconnect the last thing closed.
steps.prompt: Release the car-top switch, then the pit switch, then take your lock off the hasp, then close the main disconnect.
steps.title: Restore in the correct order
steps.why: Restore from the inside out, so that the last protection removed is the one furthest from where people were. Car top clear before the pit, pit clear before the lock, lock off before power. Each release is also a headcount — you cannot reset the pit switch without being in the pit to see it is empty. Nobody closes a disconnect that still carries a lock, and that includes the person whose lock it is.

steps.cue: With power back on, run the car on a test trip before you hand it over.
steps.prompt: With power back on, run the car on a test trip before you hand it over.
steps.title: Run a test operation before release
steps.why: The car is not returned to service on the strength of the work having gone well; it is proven with a run, in normal operation, through the floors it serves. A stop switch left half made, a hatch not latched or a safety knocked out of adjustment all behave perfectly until the car actually moves, and the person who should discover that is you, standing at the controller, not the first passenger through the doors.
